why.correct: On light sand with owls, 23 of 30 light mice (77%) survived against 10 of 30 dark mice (33%); on dark soil the pattern reversed, 21 of 30 dark (70%) against 9 of 30 light (30%). Without owls, 8 or 9 of 10 survived in every group.
options: Correct: matched mice survived at roughly twice the rate of mismatched mice when owls could hunt, and the difference disappeared without owls.
On dark soil the dark mice survived better (21 of 30 against 9 of 30), so light coats were not better on both soils.
This reverses the data: the large difference between coats appears with owls, and survival is similar without them.
Dark-coated mice survived well on dark soil; survival depended on the match between coat and soil, not on the soil alone.

why.correct: Dark: 10 ÷ 30 = 0.333. Light: 23 ÷ 30 = 0.767. Relative survival = 0.333 ÷ 0.767 = 0.43. On light sand, a dark mouse was less than half as likely as a light mouse to survive the four weeks.

The netted enclosures are a control: same soils, same mice, same time, but no owls. Survival there was high and similar for both coats, so the differences in the open enclosures can be attributed to owls.
options: Correct: removing only the owls tests whether they are the cause of the difference.
No owls could reach the netted enclosures, so they cannot show what owls choose.
The study lasted four weeks and counted adults that survived; it did not count offspring.
Coat color in adult mice is inherited and does not change to match the soil; the netting was not there to measure color change.

why.correct: Mismatched mice died at higher rates only when owls could hunt, which fits owls finding visible mice more easily. The owls are the selective pressure; coat color is the heritable trait it acts on.
options: Correct: the difference appears only with owls, and a visual predator explains why contrast matters.
Nothing in the data concerns food, and without owls both coat colors survived equally well on both soils.
This predicts the reverse of the data: mismatched mice died more, not less.
Coat color is inherited and fixed in adults; the data show differences only when owls were present.

why.correct: Dark mice survive at less than half the rate of light mice on light sand, so fewer dark parents breed, and the dark allele makes up a smaller share of each new generation.
options: Correct: differential survival, repeated each generation, shifts the proportions.
Adult mice do not change their inherited coat color in response to the soil.
Owls do not change any mouse's alleles, but they change which mice survive to pass their alleles on, so the proportions change.
A third of dark mice survive and breed, so dark mice decline over several generations rather than disappearing at once.

why.correct: The most successful type is purple, with 8.0 flowering offspring per plant, so its relative fitness is 1. White: 6.0 ÷ 8.0 = 0.75.
Pink plants make 200 seeds, but only 2.5% become flowering plants: 200 × 0.025 = 5.0. Purple plants make 80 seeds, 10% of which flower: 8.0. Surviving, reproducing offspring are what pass alleles on.
options: Correct: reproductive success is measured in offspring that survive to reproduce.
Seed number alone ignores survival; most of the pink plants' seeds never become flowering plants.
The table already follows the seeds to flowering the next year, and pink plants leave the fewest.
Small seeds lower the chance of growing (2.5%), but 5 offspring per pink plant still flowered. The key point is the count of flowering offspring, which is lowest for pink.

why.correct: Flower color is inherited and purple plants leave the most flowering offspring (8.0 per plant), so each generation has a larger share of purple plants than the one before.
options: Correct: the type with the highest fitness increases in frequency.
Seed number is not fitness; pink plants leave the fewest flowering offspring.
Sharing a meadow does not stop selection; the colors leave different numbers of offspring in that meadow.
Being intermediate does not help here: white plants leave 6.0 offspring, fewer than purple's 8.0.

why.correct: White: 120 × 2.5% = 3.0; purple: 80 × 5.0% = 4.0. Relative fitness = 3.0 ÷ 4.0 = 0.75, the same as before. Relative fitness compares types, so a change that affects all types equally does not change it.
options: Correct: halving every color's survival leaves the ratios unchanged.
White plants' offspring halve, but so do purple plants', so the ratio stays 0.75.
Survival falls by the same factor for every color, so the gap between them in relative terms does not shrink.
Relative fitness can always be calculated by dividing by the most successful type, even in a bad year.

why.correct: Selection needs variation, inheritance of that variation, and differences in survival or reproduction linked to it. With all three, the helpful version becomes more common over generations.
options: Needed: with no variation there is nothing to select among.
Needed: if the differences are not inherited, the survivors' offspring will not resemble them.
Needed: if the trait makes no difference to survival or reproduction, its frequency does not change by selection.
Not needed: selection involves no awareness or choice by individuals.
Not needed, and not true: mutations arise at random with respect to what would help.
This would remove selection: if every offspring survived and reproduced, no trait would leave more offspring than another.

why.correct: Heritable variation comes first; overproduction and a selective pressure mean not all survive; the trait affects who survives; survivors reproduce; the population's makeup shifts.

Inheritance runs through the alleles in gametes. Stretching does not change those alleles, so a stretched neck is not passed on. Selection explains long necks through inherited differences in neck length that already existed.
options: Correct: traits acquired during life are not inherited.
Necks grow after birth; the flaw is not about stretching but about inheritance.
A mutation changes one individual's alleles at random; it does not lengthen necks across a population in one generation.
Neck length is heritable; what is not inherited is a change acquired by stretching.

why.correct: Fitness is the number of offspring that survive to reproduce. The small male leaves 7, more than any other deer listed, whatever its size or lifespan.
options: Correct: 7 offspring that breed is the highest reproductive success here.
Size and a long life matter only through offspring; 3 breeding fawns is fewer than 7.
Ten fawns born, but only 2 reach breeding age, so this female's fitness is 2.
Winning fights is not fitness unless it leads to offspring; this male leaves 1.

why.correct: The selective pressure has changed, so the favored trait has changed. The population's makeup shifts over generations; no individual's alleles change.

variables.name: Proportion of newborn hares with thick fur, many generations later
variables.why: Thick-furred hares leave fewer young, so their alleles make up a smaller share of each generation.

variables.name: Number of surviving young left by a thick-furred hare compared with a thin-furred hare
variables.why: Overheating lowers the survival and breeding of thick-furred hares, which is what makes the trait less fit.

variables.name: Number of copies of the thick-fur allele in each cell of a thick-furred adult that survives
variables.why: Selection changes who survives and breeds, not the alleles inside a living individual.

variables.name: Average fur thickness of the population, many generations later
variables.why: As thin-furred hares leave more offspring, the population average shifts toward thinner fur.

why.correct: Evolution is a change in the inherited makeup of a population across generations. If the survivors' offspring, raised in the same conditions, also have larger toe pads, the difference is heritable and the next generation has shifted.
options: Correct: it shows the change is inherited and appears in the next generation.
Growth during an individual's life is not inherited, so this would weaken the claim.
This shows how survivors were selected within one generation, but not that the trait is inherited by the next.
Age differences would offer another explanation for larger pads, weakening the claim rather than supporting it.

why.correct: Darwin's phrase means that living species are the modified descendants of earlier ones; natural selection was his and Wallace's explanation of how the modification happens.
options: Correct: descent from earlier species, with change across generations.
This is inheritance of acquired traits, which Darwin's theory does not need and which does not happen.
This is the opposite of descent with modification.
Darwin's point is that species change over generations; individual lifetime changes are not inherited.

why.correct: If each pair's millions of eggs gave even a few dozen breeding adults, the population would explode. A steady size means that on average about two offspring per pair survive to breed: overproduction plus heavy losses, the conditions for selection.
options: Correct: overproduction with a steady population means most offspring die before reproducing.
Nothing in the observation suggests egg number tracks how many cod there are; the point is that most young die.
Even if many eggs go unfertilized, the number that hatch far exceeds the number that live to breed.
Fitness counts surviving offspring that reproduce, not eggs; comparing egg numbers alone says nothing about fitness.

why.correct: Selection sorts existing heritable variation; it does not create it. Tolerance can spread only if an allele for it is present or arises by a random mutation. If none does, most beetles may starve.
options: Correct: with no heritable variation in tolerance, there is nothing for selection to favor.
Need does not produce alleles; mutations arise at random.
Selection does not make alleles; mutation does, and effort does not cause mutations.
Changes made during an individual's life do not alter its gametes' DNA and are not inherited.

why.correct: A selective pressure is the feature of the environment that makes some heritable traits survive or reproduce better. Here, being caught by trout is what favors fish with more plates.
options: Correct: the trout are the environmental factor that sorts the fish.
The alleles are the source of the heritable variation that selection acts on, not the pressure.
The plates are the trait being selected, not the cause of selection.
Offspring number measures the outcome (fitness); it is not the environmental cause.

why.correct: Individuals survive and reproduce or do not; that is where selection acts. The result, a shift in which traits are common, appears in the population across generations.
options: Correct: individuals are selected, populations evolve.
An individual's inherited traits do not change; which individuals reproduce changes.
Selection's effect accumulates over generations; it does not reshape a population's individuals within one.
Selection has no goal; it favors whatever works better now, and that changes when the environment changes.

why.correct: 9.92 − 9.40 = 0.52 mm. The 1976 bar runs 9.28-9.52 mm and the 1978 bar 9.78-10.06 mm; they do not overlap, so the increase is unlikely to be chance alone.
options: Correct: a 0.52 mm rise with non-overlapping ± 2 SE bars.
The bars end at 9.52 and start at 9.78 mm, so they do not overlap.
The rise is about 0.5 mm, not 5 mm; the axis is in tenths of a millimeter.
The bars are about ± 0.1 mm wide, far smaller than the 0.5 mm change.

why.correct: Beak depth is heritable and affected survival during the drought, because only deep beaks could open the remaining seeds. Survivors were mostly deep-beaked, so their offspring had deeper beaks: directional selection.
options: Correct: differential survival in the drought, then inheritance by the next generation.
Changes gained during life are not inherited; the parents' alleles, not their experience, set the chicks' beaks.
Mutations arise at random, not because birds need them; the drought sorted birds that already differed.
The stimulus says chicks resemble their parents in beak depth whatever they are fed, which rules out diet as the cause.

why.correct: In the drought, deep beaks were favored; after the wet year, abundant small, soft seeds favored smaller beaks, which handle them efficiently, and smaller birds need less food. A trait's value depends on the environment.
options: Correct: changing food changed which beak was favorable, and selection followed.
The 1978-1982 means stayed high for years; they fell only after the food changed in 1983.
Weather does not cause specific mutations; it changes which existing beak depths survive and breed.
There is no fixed best value; the favored depth changed with the seeds available.

why.correct: Selection changes the next generation only if offspring resemble their parents. Showing that chicks resemble their parents whatever they eat links the drought survivors' beaks to the deeper beaks of the 1978 birds.
options: Correct: heritability is what carries selection on parents into the next generation.
The drought did not change any beak; it changed which birds survived to breed.
Heritable does not mean identical; chicks resemble their parents on average, with variation.
The wet years did change the population's beaks, by selection; heritability makes that possible rather than ruling it out.

why.correct: Shortened and lengthened birds were cut and glued. The cut-and-reglued birds had the same handling with no change in length, so any difference between them and the other treatments can be attributed to tail length.
options: Correct: it controls for the procedure itself.
Their tails were the normal length; the lengthened group had the longest tails.
Regrowth was not measured; the dependent variable is the number of new nests.
Every group lived on its own territory; the reglued group was not set up as a choice test.

why.correct: Lengthened: 1.7-2.9 nests; cut and reglued: 0.6-1.6. These do not overlap. Shortened: 0.2-1.0, which overlaps the reglued range, so a difference in that comparison is not shown.
options: Correct: only the lengthened group's interval is clear of the control's.
This reverses the two comparisons: the shortened interval overlaps the control, the lengthened one does not.
The cut-and-reglued and unaltered groups (0.6-1.6 and 0.7-1.7) overlap almost completely.
Error bars do not hide differences; the lengthened group's interval sits clear of the control's.

why.correct: This is sexual selection by mate choice. Fitness is offspring, not survival: a male with a long tail may die sooner but fathers more chicks, so long-tail alleles increase.
options: Correct: mating success can outweigh a survival cost.
The stimulus gives no evidence that tails help escape; the data concern mating success.
The stimulus says males' tails are several times longer than females': a sexual dimorphism.
Need does not produce traits, and individual growth in one season does not explain why the trait evolved.

why.correct: Female choice is a selective pressure on males. Over generations, male tails lengthen until the survival cost of an even longer tail balances the mating advantage.

variables.name: Mean tail length of males, over many generations
variables.why: Long-tailed males father more chicks, so the alleles for long tails become more common.

variables.name: Difference in tail length between males and females, over many generations
variables.why: The preference acts on males, so male tails lengthen while female tails are not selected the same way, widening the dimorphism.

variables.name: Natural tail length of the sons of a male whose tail was glued longer, compared with the sons of an unaltered male with the same natural tail
variables.why: Gluing raises that male's mating success but does not change his alleles, so his sons inherit the tail length his alleles code for.

why.correct: Both extremes leave more offspring than the middle, so the distribution of beak size spreads out or splits into two peaks.
options: Correct: the two extremes are favored over intermediates.
Stabilizing selection favors intermediates; here intermediates do worst.
Small beaks are favored too, so selection is not pushing in one direction.
Nothing in the example concerns mating; seeds are the selective pressure.

why.correct: This is stabilizing selection: the middle is favored and both tails are selected against, so the curve narrows around about the same mean.
options: Correct: stabilizing selection keeps the mean and trims both tails.
Heavy babies had lower survival than middle-weight babies, so the mean would not shift upward.
Two peaks result when both extremes are favored (disruptive), the opposite of this pattern.
Widening is the effect of disruptive selection; stabilizing selection narrows the spread.

why.correct: Abiotic factors are the nonliving parts of the environment: temperature and soil salt. Fungi, hawks and neighboring plants are living, so they are biotic factors.
options: Abiotic: temperature is a nonliving factor.
Abiotic: salt in the soil is a nonliving factor.
Biotic: the fungus is a living parasite.
Biotic: the hawk is a living predator.
Biotic: the neighboring plants are living competitors, even though the shade they cast is what harms seedlings.

why.correct: Cleaner air changed the bark, which changed which phenotype was favorable. Selection then reversed, and the black form became rare, as it did in Britain after the 1950s.

variables.name: Percentage of moths in the region that are black
variables.why: On pale, lichen-covered bark, birds find black moths more easily, so black moths leave fewer offspring.

variables.name: How easily birds spot a black moth resting on a tree trunk
variables.why: Black moths contrast more with pale lichen than with soot-darkened bark.

variables.name: Number of copies of the black allele in the cells of one black moth
variables.why: Selection changes which moths survive and breed, not the alleles inside a living moth.

variables.name: Survival of pale moths compared with black moths
variables.why: Pale moths now blend in with lichen, so birds take fewer of them than black moths.

why.correct: Pale: 42 ÷ 400 = 0.105. Black: 82 ÷ 400 = 0.205. Relative survival = 0.105 ÷ 0.205 = 0.51. In sooty woods, a pale moth was about half as likely as a black moth to survive the week.

A small difference in a protein (molecular variation) changes how well blood picks up oxygen, which affects survival and reproduction only where oxygen is scarce. So the variant is favorable at altitude, not in the lowlands.
options: Correct: molecular variation affects fitness in one environment and not another.
Low oxygen does not cause particular mutations; the variants arose at random and were favored where they helped.
A protein made during an individual's life is not passed on; the alleles in its gametes are.
The variants are rare in the lowlands, which suggests they bring no advantage there; favorable depends on the environment.

why.correct: With most attacks from one side, prey guard that side, so the rarer form has the advantage. Its share rises until it is no longer rare: frequency-dependent selection keeps both forms near equal.
options: Correct: the rare form is favored, so the shares swing back toward balance.
Being common is a disadvantage here, because prey guard against the common form's attacks.
Prey become watchful on the side attacked most often, so they do not guard both sides equally.
Mouth direction is inherited, not switched; selection changes the proportions of the forms.

why.correct: The models differ only in color and are placed on matching and non-matching backgrounds. If birds attack models that contrast with their background more often, color affects the risk of being eaten in the way the hypothesis predicts.
options: Correct: it manipulates color and background, controls everything else, and measures attacks by birds.
Counting caterpillars and birds on one tree has no comparison between colors and no measure of attacks.
This tests whether color changes with diet, not whether birds favor green caterpillars.
Pigment and leaf number say nothing about whether birds find green or brown caterpillars more easily.

why.correct: A regulatory change at the molecular level gives an adult a new ability, but it raises fitness only where milk is available to adults. That environment-dependent advantage explains why the alleles are common in herding populations.
options: Correct: the advantage depended on the diet, so the alleles spread where milk was eaten.
Using a gene does not change the DNA in gametes; drinking milk does not make the change heritable.
Mutations arise at random; herding made existing mutations favorable rather than causing them.
If the alleles helped equally everywhere, the pattern would not track dairying; their advantage depends on the diet.

why.correct: This is sexual selection through competition within one sex. Winning fights brings many matings, so alleles for large size spread through males, producing sexual dimorphism.
options: Correct: male-male competition favors large males.
If females chose small partners, males would not be selected to be large.
If size helped both sexes equally, it would not explain why males are so much larger than females.
Growth gained by eating is not inherited; only alleles are.

why.correct: Black wings were favored on soot-darkened bark and disfavored on lichen-covered bark. Adaptive is relative to an environment.
options: Correct: favorable depends on the environment.
Black moths were favored and then disfavored within about a century, when the bark changed.
Fitness is reproduction; a trait that lowers reproduction lowers fitness even if it helps survival.
Dark color was a disadvantage on pale, lichen-covered bark.

why.correct: High: 4.7% to 19.8% with nearly equal steps each 10 generations. Low: 4.7% to 1.8% in the first 30 generations, then only to 0.8% over the next 70.
options: Correct: a steady rise in one line, a fast fall that flattens in the other.
The low line slowed sharply after 30 generations, so it is not falling at a steady rate toward 0%.
The high line kept rising by more than 1 percentage point every 10 generations through generation 100.
This reverses the two lines: the high line kept rising, and the low line leveled off.

why.correct: Rate = (19.8 − 4.7) ÷ (100 − 0) = 15.1 ÷ 100 = 0.15 percentage points per generation.

A polygenic trait has many alleles that each add a little. Each round of selection makes some of them more common, but plenty of heritable variation is left (and mutation adds a little), so the next round can still move the mean.
options: Correct: continued response needs continued heritable variation.
Both lines grew in the same fields, so the fields cannot explain why only one line rose.
Plants do not learn, and changes in an individual are not inherited; the line changed because of which plants bred.
Choosing parents does not cause mutations; it changes which existing alleles are passed on.

why.correct: Kernels with almost no oil grow poorly, which limits how far the line can go, and once nearly every plant carries the low-oil alleles, there is little heritable variation for further selection to act on.
options: Correct: a physical limit plus used-up variation slows the response.
The method was the same for both lines every generation, as the stimulus states.
The low line did fall far below 4.7%, to 0.8%, so the starting variety did hold alleles for less oil.
Both lines were run the same way with the same number of selected ears.

why.correct: Selecting the same population in the opposite direction can only work if it still contains alleles for lower oil. A falling oil content in the reverse line shows that heritable variation remained.
options: Correct: a response to reverse selection reveals remaining heritable variation.
No change would suggest the opposite: no heritable variation left to select.
Return to the starting value in one generation would not fit selection on many genes, each with a small effect.
A continued rise under selection for low oil would mean selection was not working at all.

why.correct: 512 ÷ 2 = 256. The cells in flask 2 now survive an antibiotic concentration 256 times higher than the starting culture could.
The untreated flasks went through the same medium, transfers and number of generations, and their MIC stayed at 2 µg/mL. The only difference is the antibiotic, so it is the cause of the rise.
options: Correct: same handling, no drug, no change.
Cells survived in the treated flasks; that is how the MIC could be measured on day 24.
The untreated flasks show no rise in resistance; they do not measure mutation rates.
Every flask had an MIC of 2 µg/mL on day 0, and all came from one culture.

why.correct: Resistance mutations arise at random in a huge population. Each dose kills the less resistant cells, so the more resistant ones take over; later random mutations in those survivors can raise resistance again, giving a rise in steps.
options: Correct: random variation plus repeated selection by the drug.
Mutations are not directed at the drug's target by the drug; resistant variants are random, and the drug removes the others.
Tolerance gained by one cell during its life is not what changes the MIC; resistant mutants replace susceptible cells.
The MIC is measured on fresh samples with a set concentration, so it reflects the cells, not breakdown of the dose.

why.correct: Which resistance mutations appear, and when, is a matter of chance. Flasks started alike can follow different paths, which is evidence that the mutations were not directed by the drug.
options: Correct: random mutation makes replicate populations differ.
The doses were the same; differences between replicates are expected when mutations arise by chance.
All flasks had the same MIC on day 0, so there is no evidence that flask 2 started different.
Bacteria do not change in response to sensing a drug; random mutants are selected.

why.correct: Both change populations over generations by acting on heritable variation. The difference is the agent: human choice or the environment.
options: Correct: the difference is who or what does the choosing.
Both act on heritable variation; traits gained during life are not inherited in either.
Neither creates alleles; mutation does. Both select among existing variants.
Both change populations, not individuals.

why.correct: Choosing leaves (kale), the end bud (cabbage), flower buds (broccoli) or the stem (kohlrabi) generation after generation turned one ancestral plant into several crops that are still one species.
options: Correct: different selection on one ancestor.
They share one wild ancestor; the crops did not come from different species.
Grown side by side in one field, the crops keep their shapes, so the differences are inherited, not caused by soil.
The differences built up over many generations of selection on many genes, not from one mutation each.

why.correct: In the two correct examples, human activity changed which individuals reproduced without anyone aiming to change the population: fishing and poaching. Choosing parents for a wanted trait is deliberate artificial selection.
options: Unintended: removing large fish favors fish that breed young and small.
Unintended: poachers killed tusked elephants, so tuskless ones bred more.
Intended: choosing seed for big fruit is deliberate artificial selection.
Intended: choosing calm horses as parents is deliberate artificial selection.
Intended: picking the fastest-growing trout as parents is deliberate artificial selection.

why.correct: Resistance alleles arise by random mutation or gene transfer. The antibiotic is the selective pressure: it removes susceptible cells, so the resistant ones take over.
options: Correct: the drug selects; it does not create resistance.
Bacteria do not mutate on demand; mutations arise at random.
No organism changes its alleles because it needs to; bacteria evolve fast because of their numbers and short generations.
Resistance is a property of the bacteria, measured by their survival at a given drug concentration.

why.correct: Billions of cells mean rare resistance mutations are present somewhere; generations of minutes mean selection repeats many times a day; and plasmids passed by conjugation spread resistance genes between cells.
options: Correct: numbers, generation time and gene transfer.
Mammals do vary genetically; complexity is not why bacteria evolve fast.
Mammals have plenty of heritable variation; their generations are just far longer.
Neither evolves on purpose; random variation is selected in both.

why.correct: When one gene affects several traits (pleiotropy), or genes for different traits are linked, selecting one trait shifts the others. Changes in hormones and development linked to tameness are thought to alter ears and coat color.
options: Correct: correlated traits changed because shared genes were selected.
The question says the breeders selected only for calmness; nothing suggests hidden choices.
Changes during an individual's life are not inherited.
Need does not cause mutations; the traits rose because they were tied to selected genes.

why.correct: Harvesting itself selected for seeds that stay on the plant, even before anyone chose it on purpose, and deliberate choice increased kernel number. Domesticated corn cannot spread its seeds well without people.

variables.name: Proportion of plants whose seeds stay on the ear until harvest
variables.why: Seeds that stayed on the plant were the ones harvested and planted, so the alleles for holding seeds were passed on.

variables.name: Mean number of kernels per ear
variables.why: Farmers chose seed from the ears with the most kernels, so alleles for more kernels became more common.

variables.name: Number of chromosomes in each plant cell
variables.why: Selecting among plants changes which alleles are common, not the chromosome number.

variables.name: Ability of the plants to spread their own seeds without people
variables.why: Plants that held their seeds were favored, so the crop came to depend on people to sow it.

why.correct: Resistant: 4 × 10⁸ ÷ 10⁶ = 400 cells. Susceptible survivors: 0.1% of about 4 × 10⁸ = 4 × 10⁵ = 400,000 cells. Resistant share = 400 ÷ (400 + 400,000) × 100 = 0.0999% ≈ 0.1%, up from 0.0001% before treatment: a thousand-fold enrichment in one day.
Shooting large-horned rams before they bred removed their alleles from the population, so the rams that bred were mostly smaller-horned: unintended selection.
options: Correct: the hunters changed which rams reproduced.
Stress during life does not explain a change in the heritable trait across generations.
Rams cannot change their horns because of danger; the change came from which rams bred.
Horn size is heritable, and the decline over generations shows the hunting did select.

why.correct: With few founding dogs and frequent matings between relatives, two parents often carry the same rare recessive allele, so more puppies inherit two copies and show the disease.
options: Correct: matings among relatives raise the share of homozygous recessive puppies.
Some breed traits do carry health costs, but breeders did not select for disease; homozygosity explains most inherited disorders.
Mutation rates do not depend on whether a dog is purebred.
These are inherited diseases, passed by alleles, not infections passed by contact.

why.correct: Breeders showed that choosing which individuals reproduce, generation after generation, changes populations dramatically. Darwin argued that the environment does the same choosing in nature.
options: Correct: it demonstrates the power of selection on heritable variation.
Breeding works by choosing parents, not by individuals changing their traits.
Dog breeds and crops are still one species each; breeding shows change within a species.
Selection changes a population only if the trait is heritable.

why.correct: S1 reached 1 by generation 15 and S2 reached 0 by generation 11, while S3 wandered between 0.2 and 0.65; L1 and L2 stayed between about 0.45 and 0.56.
options: Correct: wide random swings in the small populations, little change in the large ones.
S2 fell to 0 and S3 ended at 0.4, so not every population rose toward 1.
This reverses the populations: the small ones swung widely, the large ones barely moved.
S1 rose to 1 while S2 fell to 0, and both large populations stayed near 0.5, so there is no common direction.

why.correct: This is genetic drift. Each generation is a random sample of the last one's alleles, and small samples stray much further from the true proportion than large ones, just as 10 coin tosses stray from half heads more than 1,000 do.
options: Correct: the size of the random sample sets how strong drift is.
The allele has no known effect on fitness, and two small populations went in opposite directions, which selection would not do.
Mutation rates do not depend on population size, and mutation is far too rare to move frequencies this fast.
The stimulus describes separate populations with no exchange of flies.

why.correct: Selection in identical conditions would push the same allele the same way in every population. S1 rising to 1 while S2, identical in size and conditions, fell to 0 shows the direction was random: drift.
options: Correct: opposite outcomes in identical replicates point to chance.
Reaching 1 is what the student's claim predicts, so it does not refute it.
One early dip is consistent with either drift or weak selection, so it is weak evidence.
Large populations staying near 0.5 fits no strong selection, but the two small populations are the more direct test, because they differ only by chance.

why.correct: Ten diploid flies carry 2 × 10 = 20 copies of the gene. 0.40 × 20 = 8 copies of e. With so few copies, gaining or losing just one copy changes the frequency by 0.05.
Drift removes variation within each population and increases differences between populations, faster in small ones.

variables.name: Share of heterozygous (Ee) flies in population S1
variables.why: Allele e is already fixed in S1, so every fly is ee and there are no heterozygotes to lose; without mutation or gene flow, nothing changes.

variables.name: Share of heterozygous flies in population S3
variables.why: Drift will eventually fix or lose e in S3 too, and as it nears 0 or 1, fewer flies carry both alleles.

variables.name: Spread of allele frequencies among the five populations
variables.why: Drift sends each population its own random way, and the large ones slowly drift apart as well, so they become more different from each other.

why.correct: (5.2 − 3.1) ÷ 5.2 × 100 = 2.1 ÷ 5.2 × 100 = 40.4%. Two in every five alleles present in 1960, on average, had been lost by 1990.

As the population shrank to a few dozen birds, drift raised some harmful recessive alleles to high frequencies, and close relatives mated more often. More embryos were homozygous for these alleles and failed to develop.
options: Correct: small size raised homozygosity for harmful recessive alleles.
Clutch size does not determine what percentage of laid eggs hatch.
Plowing does not cause particular mutations; the problem was the alleles already present becoming homozygous.
Seventy displaying males in 1999 gave 92% hatching, so the number of males alone does not explain the failures.

why.correct: The released birds came from large populations that still held many alleles. Breeding with them raised alleles per gene from 3.1 to 5.0 and made offspring heterozygous at more genes, masking harmful recessive alleles.
options: Correct: gene flow restored variation and lowered homozygosity.

More frequent counts make the size estimate more precise, but do not separate gene flow from habitat work.
The source populations did not receive the habitat work or the birds, so they do not test either cause here.

options: Correct: count alleles, not individuals.

(20 + 10) ÷ 50 = 0.60 counts each heterozygote as a whole d, double-counting its one copy.

why.correct: Microevolution is a change in allele frequencies in a population across generations.
options: Correct: allele frequencies in a population changed over generations.
Growth happens within one individual's life and does not change the population's alleles.
A color change in one lizard is a response of its phenotype, not a change in the population's alleles.
Regrowing a tail is a change in one individual, not in the gene pool.

why.correct: Mating with relatives or with oneself pairs like alleles more often, so homozygotes become more common and heterozygotes rarer, but the alleles themselves are passed on in the same proportions.
options: Correct: nonrandom mating rearranges alleles into genotypes without changing their frequencies.
Gene flow brings in alleles in different proportions, which changes allele frequencies.
Drift changes allele frequencies at random.

why.correct: Variation is added by gene flow, which brings in alleles the population lacks, and by mutation, which creates new alleles. Bottlenecks, matings among relatives and continued drift all reduce it.
options: Adds variation: immigrants bring alleles from a larger gene pool.
Adds variation: mutation is the source of new alleles, though it is slow.
Reduces it: a bottleneck leaves a few survivors carrying only some of the alleles.
Reduces heterozygosity: matings among relatives make more individuals homozygous.
Reduces it: drift in a small population keeps fixing or losing alleles.

why.correct: A few hundred founders are a small sample of the European population they came from. One couple happened to carry the allele, and with few founders and marriages within the community, it reached a high frequency by drift.
options: Correct: chance sampling at the founding, then drift in a small population.
The allele causes a disorder; nothing suggests it raised fitness.
The community mostly married within itself, which limits gene flow.
Ways of life do not raise the rate of a particular mutation; the allele was present at the founding.

why.correct: A bottleneck is drift: the few survivors are a chance sample, and alleles they did not carry are gone. A growing population multiplies the alleles it has; replacing lost ones needs new mutations, which accumulate very slowly.
options: Correct: numbers recover quickly, alleles do not.
Drift is weaker in large populations, so growth slows further loss but does not reverse it.
Hunting removed individuals at random with respect to their alleles; it did not cause mutations.
Genetic variation is alleles, not learned traits.

why.correct: Gene flow mixes the two gene pools. Pollen from the clean-soil plants carries sensitivity alleles into the mine population each generation, opposing selection there, so tolerance stays less common, especially near the mine's edge.
options: Correct: gene flow can work against local adaptation.
The clean-soil plants mostly lack tolerance alleles, so their pollen lowers tolerance on the mine.
Selection removes many sensitive seedlings, but new sensitive alleles keep arriving, so they are never all gone; the balance is lower tolerance.
The wind carries pollen onto the mine, so little gene flow goes the other way, and tolerance gives no advantage on clean soil anyway.

why.correct: Genetic variation is the raw material for adapting to change. A population whose members are nearly identical may lack any individuals able to survive a new threat.
options: Correct: lost variation reduces a population's ability to respond to change.
Cheetahs do reproduce; low variation raises risk, but a decline is not certain.
Mutation rates do not rise because variation is low.
The opposite: grafts are accepted because the cheetahs are so alike; grafts are not a threat in the wild.

why.correct: Both change allele frequencies across generations. Drift does so by chance and can spread harmful alleles; selection consistently favors alleles that raise survival and reproduction.
options: Correct: chance versus fitness.
Drift is strongest in small populations, and selection acts in populations of any size.
Neither creates alleles; mutation does.
Both change populations; neither changes an individual's alleles.

why.correct: A small chance sample of founders, then drift while the population is small, can make a rare allele common, with no role for fitness.

Mating with relatives produces fewer heterozygotes, not more.

p + q always equals 1; equilibrium is judged by whether genotype counts match p², 2pq, q², and they do not.

options: Correct: q holds steady at about 0.50.
q falls from 0.50 to 0.05 because aa beetles are removed: selection.
q falls toward 0.10, the frequency in the stock supplying replacement beetles: gene flow.
q wanders between 0.40 and 0.80 at random: drift in a population of 10.

options: Correct: selection against a recessive phenotype weakens as the allele becomes rare.
The share of aa offspring falls because q falls, not because beetles adapt to the procedure.

Nothing removes allele a in population 3, and the incoming beetles carry it at 0.10.

Analogous: insect wings are not modified limbs, while bird wings are.

Changes during life are not inherited, and climate does not explain the resemblance to South America.
The species are unique to the islands and older than human visits; nothing suggests they came from Africa.
